post.originalText:
Asked Gemini 4 Argon to visualize Earth’s entire 4.54-billion-year history.

My main requirement: scientific accuracy.

Then I asked it to break down what the visualization is actually based on:

>Present day - GSHHG coastlines and NOAA ETOPO 2022 elevation on a 60-arc-second grid (~1.85 km between grid points at the equator). NASA Blue Marble surface imagery is from 2004.

>The last 80,000 years - ice-sheet data from the PaleoMIST 1.0 reconstruction, at 2,500-year intervals. The steps between those snapshots are interpolated.

>540 million years ago to today - PALEOMAP / Scotese & Wright paleogeography, interpolated between map snapshots.

>1.8 billion to 540 million years ago - CAO2024 continental-block reconstruction. Ancient positions are uncertain; coastlines and relief are illustrative.

>Earlier Earth and the Moon-forming impact - visual reconstructions, not a literal geophysical simulation.

The further back in time you go, the more the visualization relies on reconstruction rather than direct geographic data. 

https://t.co/geeKA5a4iQ

sourceMaterials.text: @knowixbuilds Probably, but I’m sure Opus would’ve done a better job. It took a couple of hours, there were too many collision issues, and I still don’t like how it turned out

×ABOUT THE RECONSTRUCTIONA planet across deep time.

Modern surface: NASA Blue Marble, GSHHG coastlines and NOAA ETOPO 2022 relief.
Last 80,000 years: PaleoMIST 1.0.
Last 540 million years: PALEOMAP PaleoDEM.
Back to 1.8 billion years ago: CAO2024 continental blocks.

Early Earth, ancient clouds, fine surface detail, colours and Cryogenian ice fronts are illustrative. Theia represents the giant-impact hypothesis for lunar formation. The approach follows two-body gravity; melt flow, ejecta and lunar assembly are visual reconstructions. Later impacts are representative examples. Ancient maps are interpolated; this is not a physical tectonics simulator.

Space Play / pauseH Clean viewC CloudsF Full screenL LightingR Reset camera

Drag to orbit. Scroll or pinch to zoom. Studio light keeps the visible globe readable; sunlight preserves day and night.
The timeline is nonlinear. The 60-second journey uses ten paced chapters. Land imagery dates to August 2004; cloud imagery to July 2001. This is not live weather.
